docs.preview:
# Contributing

You like WebdriverIO and want to help making it better? Awesome! We are working to make this process as easy and transparent as possible. We might be not quite there yet but this guide will help you to ramp you up as a contributor and give you everything you need to make your first contribution. If there is any information missing that prevents you from sending in a pull request, please let us know. We treat these kind of issues like actual bugs.

## Code of Conduct

Everyone who participates in this project, either as a user or a contributor, is obliged to follow the projects [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/webdriverio/webdriverio/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). Every violation against it will be reviewed and investigated and will result in a response that is deemed necessary and appropriate to the circumstances. The project team is obligated to maintain confidentiality with regard to the reporter of an incident. Further details of specific enforcement policies may be posted separately.

## Find A Way To Contribute

The project offers a variety of ways to contribute. If you struggle to find something suited for you, join the WebdriverIO [support channel](https://discord.webdriver.io) on Matrix and reach out to the maintainer there. Don't be shy, they are there to help!

You can participate by:

- contributing code
- improving documentation
- answer questions and provide help in the [Discord](https://discord.webdriver.io) support channel
- create educational content (blog posts, tutorials, videos, etc.)
- spread the good word about the project (e.g. via Twitter)
- create bugs if you discover them while using WebdriverIO
- make feature requests if you are missing something in the project
- if you'd like to support us monetarily, consider [donating to the project](https://webdriver.io/community/donate)

The maintainers of the project try to organize all [issues](https://github.com/webdriverio/webdriverio/issues) in the way that should allow anyone to have enough context to start working on it. If this is not the case please mention it in the issue thread so that either the issue creator or a maintainer can provide more information.

If you want to contribute code, a general good first way to find a task to work on is to look into all tickets with the label [`help wanted`](https://github.com/webdriverio/webdriverio/labels/help%20wanted) and/or [`good first pick`](https://github.com/webdriverio/webdriverio/issues?q=is%3Aopen+label%3A%22good+first+pick%22+sort%3Aupdated-desc). All these tickets are up for grab if they haven't a user assigned to them. If you find something that interests you, ensure to let us know in the issue thread that you have the intend to work on it.

Often issues require some amount of context to the problem which makes it difficult to get an idea about what needs to be done. Depending on your experience using / working with the project this context can be missing. Often it helps to start with tasks around missing documentation or just increase test coverage of some parts in the code. After some time you will get more familiar with the codebase which allows you to pick up more difficult tasks.

If you can't find something that suits you, look into the [project roadmap](https://github.com/webdriverio/webdriverio/blob/main/ROADMAP.md) to see if there is something interesting for you. At the end you can also _always_ reach out to the maintainers in the [Discord](https://discord.webdriver.io) support channel. They are responsible to find a task for you.

## Reporting New Issues

When [opening a new issue](https://github.com/webdriverio/webdriverio/issues/new/choose), always make sure to fill out the issue template. __This step is very important!__ Not doing so may result in your issue not managed in a timely fashion. Don't take this personally if this happens, and feel free to open a new issue once you've gathered all the information required by the template.

- __One issue, one bug:__ Please report a single bug per issue.
- __Provide reproduction steps:__ List all the steps necessary to reproduce the issue. The person reading your bug report should be able to follow these steps to reproduce your issue with minimal effort.

### Providing a reproducible example

A reproducible example is a simple, self-contained script or program that demonstrates the issue or bug you're experiencing. The goal is to allow others to recreate the problem easily and efficiently.

Steps to Create a Reproducible Example:

1. Isolate the Problem:
- Narrow down your code to the smallest amount that still reproduces the issue.
- Remove any non-essential code or dependencies that are not related to the problem.

2. Ensure that others can run your example and reproduce the issue:
- It should not require any non-standard setup unless absolutely necessary, e.g. remove any need for special software or services like CI vendors.
- Document steps necessary to execute the reproducible example

3. Share project
- Create a new public GitHub repository and push your reproducible example to it.
- Share the link to the repository in the issue.
- Document what behavior you observe and what behavior you would expect

__Note:__ if you can't provide a reproducible example we unfortunately are forced to close the issue.

### Security Bugs

See [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/webdriverio/webdriverio/blob/main/.github/SECURITY.md).

## Flowcharts

The flowcharts provide a high level overview of the WebdriverIO ecosystem and how the different packages interact with each other.

[WDIO Commands](https://webdriver.io/docs/flowcharts/wdiocommands) - Explains the wdio config, install and repl command workflows.

[Create local worker process](https://webdriver.io/docs/flowcharts/createlocalworkerprocess) - Explains the interaction between the @wdio/cli, @wdio/local-runner and @wdio/runner packages and how a worker process is created.

[Test execution](https://webdriver.io/docs/flowcharts/testexecution) - Overview of how the tests are run in the local runner worker process.

[High level overview](https://webdriver.io/docs/flowcharts/highleveloverview) - Flow chart provides a high level overview of how the WebdriverIO ecosystem interacts with the core packages.

## Proposing a Change

We are happy for every idea you have that improves the usability of the framework. If you have an idea about a new feature please raise a [feature request](https://github.com/webdriverio/webdriverio/issues/new?template=--feature-request.md) first to get feedback by the maintainer team on it. This lets us reach an agreement on your proposal before you put significant effort into it.

If you’re only fixing a bug, it’s fine to submit a pull request right away, but we still recommend to file an issue detailing what you’re fixing. This is helpful in case we don’t accept that specific fix but want to keep track of the issue.

### Work With The Code

If you make any changes to the code, you want to test it quickly to see if they do what you expect. There are a couple of ways to do that in WebdriverIO. For one, you can link single sub-packages into your own project to see if the changes you've made have the effect you expected.

Another way to test changes in WebdriverIO is by using its [example directory](https://github.com/webdriverio/webdriverio/tree/main/examples) or by running its [smoke test suite](https://github.com/webdriverio/webdriverio/tree/main/tests). The example directory is a set of sample scripts that use WebdriverIO in various ways. Here, you need to have a browser driver running to run the scripts. With the smoke test suite you can run various flavors of WebdriverIO within a predefined execution scenario. All of these scenarios are defined in our [WebDriver Mock Service](https://github.com/webdriverio/webdriverio/tree/main/packages/wdio-webdriver-mock-service) that mimics a browser driver by stubbing the endpoints with predefined responses. It is a great way to run WebdriverIO suites quickly without having to setup anything.

### Make a Pull Request

Once you have a fix implemented or finished a feature implementation you can make a pull request. Your changes

report.overview: WebdriverIO is a Node.js automation framework for developers testing websites, browser components, and mobile applications through WebDriver, WebDriver BiDi, and Appium. This monorepo combines standalone browser clients, a CLI that schedules isolated test workers, framework adapters, services, reporters, and a Vite-based browser runner. Its distinctive architecture layers resilient element commands and session managers over protocol bindings while allowing runners, commands, locators, and integrations to be extended.
report.agent_prompt:
Onboard to the WebdriverIO monorepo at commit dbf0f497130676040ce4212d9cf6459adfe16c42. Treat this brief as a bounded source investigation, not exhaustive coverage or proof that tests pass. Tests and GitHub Actions were inspected, not executed. Verify the checkout and current instructions before working; preserve read-only restrictions unless the task explicitly authorizes execution or changes. Never inspect secrets, environment files, credentials, or keys.

Start with package.json, pnpm-workspace.yaml, tsconfig.json, vitest.config.ts, and the owning package manifest. The root selects pnpm 10.34.5 and uses an internal esbuild compiler. Public packages expose different Node, browser, ESM, and CommonJS entrypoints; changing a shared implementation can affect several export conditions. Read infra/compiler/src/index.ts before modifying build behavior. The root build performs cleanup, protocol generation, and ordered compilation, so it is not a harmless validation command.

For standalone automation, follow packages/webdriverio/src/index.ts: remote validates configuration, selects a protocol driver, creates a browser prototype, opens a session, and registers session managers. Then read packages/webdriver/src/index.ts and utils.ts for driver startup, capability normalization, POST /session, BiDi negotiation, and optional Appium direct connection. Protocol commands are generated from endpoint descriptors; command.ts validates arguments and delegates HTTP requests through environment-specific request classes.

For CLI behavior, follow packages/wdio-cli/bin/wdio.js, src/run.ts, src/commands/run.ts, and src/launcher.ts. Configuration files execute as modules. Launcher owns scheduling, instance limits, worker hooks, retries, and final exit status. Local workers inherit environment settings and communicate over Node IPC. Read packages/wdio-runner/src/index.ts before changing lifecycle order: a stub browser precedes framework discovery, beforeSession can alter retry configuration, and the real session starts only when tests exist. Preserve session teardown and reporter synchronization behavior.

For element changes, trace browser.$ through findElement and getElement, then elementErrorHandler, implicitWait, and the command implementation. BiDi lookup tracks contexts and shadow roots, checks containment and connectivity, and falls back to Classic in specified cases. Preserve selector identity and parent links because stale-element recovery depends on them. Screenshot persistence delegates through the Node environment, validates the destination directory, selects Classic or BiDi capture, decodes base64, and writes to the caller-selected path.

Extensions use command export barrels, addCommand/overwriteCommand, locator strategy maps, protocol factories, and initializePlugin. Services distinguish launcher and worker exports; shouldLoad can suppress worker imports. BrowserRunner extends LocalRunner, starts Vite servers, and supports Mocha in the browser. Shared-store state lives in a loopback HTTP server and is not durable storage.

If execution becomes authorized, begin with the smallest relevant package test selected through Vitest, then expand to applicable typing, smoke, browser, or e2e checks. Inspect mocks and CI gates first: unit tests skip driver setup, coverage is disabled by default, selected component scripts are intentionally bypassed, and cloud tests are gated to main. Report exactly what was inspected or executed and avoid interpreting test existence as success.

system_map.summary: The product is a collection of cooperating packages rather than one deployed application. Standalone clients and CLI test execution share protocol bindings but have different lifecycle owners. Node workers, real browsers, driver processes, and optional cloud backends form the principal runtime boundaries. Build artifacts are published as packages, while the documentation website has a separate deployment workflow.

claims.claim: The private ESM root workspace selects pnpm 10.34.5; workspace membership includes packages, compiler infrastructure, website, e2e, typing fixtures, and selected examples.
webdriverio exposes browser, Node ESM, and CommonJS entrypoints; its Node source installs filesystem-backed helpers and process environment access into the shared environment object.
The webdriver package owns session creation and protocol composition: WebDriver.newSession starts a driver, negotiates capabilities, constructs a client monad, and optionally connects BiDi.
The wdio executable imports the compiled CLI; run() dispatches registered commands or treats a configuration path as the default run command.
Launcher owns capability scheduling and worker capacity; local workers execute @wdio/runner and exchange commands and results through Node IPC.
BrowserRunner extends LocalRunner, requires Mocha, starts Vite servers for worker runs, registers a server-worker communicator, and aggregates coverage during shutdown.
The inspected storage boundaries are caller-selected artifact files and an optional process-memory shared store served over loopback HTTP.

Root scripts define build, unit, typing, smoke, component, and e2e checks; CI uploads compiled package artifacts, manual publishing invokes Lerna, and documentation deployment invokes the separate docs pipeline.

feature_catalog.summary: The inspected public surface spans direct automation APIs and configuration-driven test execution. Browser and element command barrels expose navigation, inspection, interaction, waiting, emulation, and artifact operations. Mobile commands and cloud endpoint selection extend the same client model beyond desktop browsers. Browser component testing, network mocking, snapshots, and shared resource pools have explicit runtime conditions.

claims.claim: remote creates a session, attach wraps an existing session, and multiremote coordinates named browser sessions; multiremote initialization opens constituent sessions concurrently.
The CLI registers config, install, repl, and run; run accepts suite/spec selection, exclusions, repetition, sharding, headless mode, watch mode, snapshot updates, and CPU/heap profiling options.
Browser exports include URL/window/frame navigation, cookies, synchronous/asynchronous script execution, keyboard and pointer actions, viewport sizing, emulation, throttling, and Puppeteer access.

Element exports include value entry, clicking, dragging, selection, text/attribute/CSS inspection, accessibility role/label retrieval, state checks, shadow/React selectors, and explicit wait commands.
Mobile exports cover native/webview contexts, app lifecycle, deep links, gestures, clipboard, device locking, connectivity controls, biometrics, and emulator telephony/power operations.
detectBackend selects BrowserStack, TestingBot, Sauce Labs, or LambdaTest defaults using credential shape and provider options; explicit connection values can override those defaults.
Browser component testing uses Vite and documented React, Preact, Vue, Svelte, Solid, and Stencil presets; the implementation rejects frameworks other than Mocha.

BiDi-only browser.mock replaces identical mock definitions; screenshot capture supports Classic PNG or BiDi PNG/JPEG options, while runner services supply snapshots, soft assertions, and shared-store get/set/resource-pool APIs.

data_flow.summary: Configuration is executable input that becomes launcher scheduling state and is reconstructed in each worker. Session requests transform requested capabilities into negotiated capabilities and protocol-specific client state. Element lookup preserves references and selectors so middleware can recover from missing or stale elements. Outputs cross distinct boundaries: IPC reporting, driver HTTP/WebSocket traffic, local artifact files, and optional loopback shared-store requests.

claims.claim: ConfigParser.initialize loads the configuration module once, merges overrides, and applies CLI headless settings; addConfigFile extracts capabilities and hooks before deep-merging remaining configuration.
getSpecs resolves configured files, applies capability specs unless CLI --spec is present, combines requested suites, deduplicates, conditionally repeats, filters exclusions, and then shards.
Launcher structured-clones capabilities for each worker, runs onWorkerStart hooks, and passes configuration path, selected specs, credentials, execArgv, and retries to runner.run.

startWebDriverSession converts flat capabilities to alwaysMatch/firstMatch, requests BiDi except for enforced Classic or Safari, normalizes overlaps, sends POST /session, and writes negotiated capabilities back to params.
Protocol command wrappers validate arguments, encode endpoint variables, construct an unmasked request body, produce masked event/log payloads, and delegate execution to environment.value.Request.

getElement converts protocol references into client objects containing elementId, selector, parent, and optional BiDi locator; the element command wrapper uses these fields for waiting and stale-reference recovery.

Worker browser command/result events become reporter events; BaseReporter fans out events, sends output through IPC when available, and shutdown waits for reporter synchronization before emitting exit.

Shared-store launcher startup injects the server port into capabilities; worker service setup installs browser.sharedStore, whose client serializes JSON over loopback HTTP into an object store or resource-pool Map.

behavior_traces.summary: Three concrete flows were followed through implementation: CLI test execution, element lookup and click, and screenshot persistence. Startup includes configuration import, worker scheduling, framework discovery, session creation, and teardown. Element interaction changes behavior according to runner environment, protocol support, and error conditions. Screenshot persistence separates capture selection from filesystem output.

claims.claim: Startup 1: wdio.js imports the compiled CLI → run() parses commands → the run handler checks the configuration path and resolves TypeScript settings → launch() constructs Launcher and calls run(); --watch instead enters Watcher.watch().

Startup 2: Launcher.run → initialize/ConfigParser.initialize → runner plugin construction → launcher services → runner.initialize → user and service onPrepare hooks → driver/browser setup → _runMode/_runSpecs → _startInstance and runner.run.

Startup 3: worker IPC dispatch invokes Runner.run → worker config import → stub session → worker services and beforeSession → reporters/framework discovery → real _initSession when tests exist → before hook → framework.run → endSession outside watch mode → snapshot IPC → _shutdown.

Action 1: browser.$ delegates string selectors through globalThis.wdio in browser-runner mode; otherwise it calls findElement and getElement. Eligible BiDi string lookups use findDeepElement, while regular lookups dispatch findElement or findElementFromElement.

Action 2: getElement installs elementErrorHandler(wrapCommand) → implicitWait waits and requeries missing elements except explicit waits/state checks and selected native scroll operations → middleware updates elementId → command executes; non-interactable and stale failures enter separate recovery branches.

Action 3: click without options calls elementClick → POST /session/:sessionId/element/:elementId/click → request.makeRequest; intercepted clicks scroll to center and retry. Options instead build pointer move/down/pause/up actions and honor skipRelease.

Persistence 1: browser.saveScreenshot → environment.value.saveScreenshot installed by node.ts → Node saveScreenshot checks filepath type → path.resolve → assertDirectoryExists → chooses takeScreenshotClassic or takeScreenshotBidi.

Persistence 2: Classic validates PNG/no options and calls takeScreenshot; BiDi obtains context/tree, validates format/quality/clip, and uses an html element screenshot inside an iframe or browsingContextCaptureScreenshot otherwise. The returned base64 becomes a Buffer, fs.writeFile persists it, and the Buffer is returned.

testing_signals.summary: Tests and CI were inspected, not executed; their existence does not establish passing results. The bounded inspection found Vitest unit tests, type compilation fixtures, a custom smoke harness, real-browser e2e suites, and component tests. Mock-heavy unit coverage is complemented by selected integration tests, but configuration deliberately suppresses some error and coverage signals. CI execution depends on changed paths, branch, operating system, and selected matrix mode.

claims.claim: The inspected unit suite uses Vitest and packages/**/*.test.ts, globally installs a fetch mock, and sets WDIO_SKIP_DRIVER_SETUP=1; this investigation produced no unit-test execution result.

Unit configuration sets dangerouslyIgnoreUnhandledErrors and typecheck.ignoreSourceErrors, disables coverage by default, and excludes the BiDi handler from coverage; watermark values are configured but are not evidence of achieved coverage.

Screenshot unit tests mock filesystem access/writes and browser capture calls; inspected cases cover Classic options rejection, BiDi iframe/full-page/clip behavior, and invalid format, extension, quality, or clip inputs.

Request tests mock Undici and fetch, then assert fresh timeout signals across retries, preservation of transformRequest signals, per-session dispatcher reuse, and cleanup specifically on session deletion.

Launcher tests mock config, logging, and driver setup; inspected test declarations cover retry requeue ordering, worker limits, grouped specs, hooks, and shutdown. Shared-store tests instead explicitly start a server and issue fetch requests.

The smoke harness runs selected tests sequentially in CI and all tests concurrently locally without a filter; contributor documentation explains that its mock WebDriver service supplies predefined driver responses.

Real-browser examples include DOM snapshots and masked input, while React component tests render and click a component. However, the Preact and miscellaneous component scripts use successful echo commands before ||, bypassing their wdio commands.

Inspected CI selects suites by changed paths, uses full or reduced Node/OS unit matrices, gates cloud tests to main, and builds English plus Arabic documentation. Typing checks compile webdriver, webdriverio, Mocha, Jasmine, and Cucumber fixtures; none of these checks was executed here.

risk_map.summary: These are source observations and explicitly labeled hypotheses, not confirmed vulnerabilities. The most consequential boundaries accept executable configuration, launch processes, communicate with drivers, and write caller-selected artifacts. Credential transport and logging depend on protocol and masking choices. Testing configuration and browser compatibility branches also create limits on what source inspection alone can establish.

claims.claim: Configuration and plugins are executable inputs: ConfigParser imports the selected config module, initializePlugin imports scoped/absolute or convention-derived modules, and automationProtocol can select a dynamically imported driver.

Process-launch boundaries inherit environment settings and accept runtime arguments; Chromium startup can download/select a driver binary, defaults allowedOrigins to '*' and allowedIps to '0.0.0.0', and accepts spawnOpts overrides.

BiDi connection options follow up to ten redirects and forward custom headers; strictSSL=false disables certificate verification. The source explicitly identifies cross-host credential forwarding as a consequence of misconfigured redirects.

HTTP session authentication uses a Basic header on /session. LambdaTest auto-detection defaults to HTTP port 80 unless overridden, and enabled Appium direct connection replaces host/protocol/path/port from returned capabilities.
Input masking covers selected request/log payloads, but command result values are logged; the e2e masked-input example explicitly warns that a later getValue exposes the password in logs.

Screenshot writes resolve caller paths without a repository-root constraint. BrowserRunner.initialize recursively removes an existing configured reports directory when clean is absent or true, so artifact configuration controls filesystem effects.

Shared-store routes bind to loopback and expose get/set/pool operations without authentication middleware in the inspected chain. validateBody checks only paths ending /get or /set, while the primary setter is POST /; this mismatch warrants investigation, not a confirmed exploit claim.

Hypothesis: compatibility regressions may escape narrow mocked checks because locator behavior combines protocol fallbacks, browser-version workarounds, shadow-root state, and stale-element recovery, while unit configuration suppresses unhandled-error and default coverage signals.

extension_points.summary: Extension is built into both user configuration and package internals. Name-based plugin loading supports official and community packages, while service activation distinguishes launcher and worker responsibilities. Command barrels and protocol descriptor tables construct client APIs. Custom locators, framework adapters, reporters, automation drivers, and compiler plugins provide additional integration seams.

claims.claim: initializePlugin resolves scoped or absolute imports first, then @wdio/<name>-<type>, then wdio-<name>-<type>, and throws an actionable error when no candidate loads.
Services accept existing hook objects, classes, or package names; package launcher exports run in the parent, and shouldLoad(config, caps) can prevent a package from being imported into workers.
Browser and element commands enter their scopes through export barrels; applyScopePrototype enumerates those exports and excludes names listed in IGNORED_COMMAND_FILE_EXPORTS.
addCommand and overwriteCommand are propagated across multiremote instances; runner session replacement also preserves custom and overwritten commands registered against the preliminary stub.
addLocatorStrategyHandler stores named functions in a strategies Map, rejects duplicate names, and propagates registrations to multiremote constituent instances.
automationProtocol selects the Driver factory or protocol stub; protocol getPrototype converts endpoint/method descriptor entries into command functions rather than hand-writing each HTTP method.

Local framework adapters load through initializePlugin(config.framework, 'framework') and expose init/run behavior; reporter configuration accepts custom classes or tuples with options and supports asynchronous synchronization.

The compiler has package-specific esbuild plugin tables, including protocol type generation, create-wdio template copying, and webdriverio external scripts; BiDi generation derives TypeScript definitions and command methods from CDDL.

agent_handoff.summary: Begin with the owning package and the smallest relevant lifecycle chain; the inventory and investigation are bounded. Tests and CI were inspected, not executed, and no passing status is asserted. Preserve the distinctions between Node/browser exports, launcher/worker hooks, stub/real sessions, and Classic/BiDi behavior. Proposed validation should remain read-only here and become executable only under appropriate task authorization.

claims.claim: Use package.json and pnpm-workspace.yaml as the dependency/build authority; tsconfig selects strict NodeNext/ES2022 compilation, and public webdriverio exports require awareness of Node, browser, ESM, and CommonJS surfaces.
For CLI lifecycle changes, read commands/run.ts, Launcher.run/_runSpecs/_endHandler, and Runner.run first; preserve hook order and the retry-budget message sent before requesting a real session.

For element behavior, keep changes within the command and relevant lookup/middleware chain; selector, parent, elementId, and BiDi locator fields are functional recovery state rather than incidental metadata.
Treat Classic and BiDi as explicit branches: findElement excludes iframe/deep-selector cases from its BiDi path, and screenshot options are rejected in Classic but validated and supported in BiDi.
Do not interpret root build/setup as passive checks: scripts clean artifacts and generate BiDi sources, whose generator can download specification input and overwrite generated TypeScript files.

If execution is later authorized, select the owning test through the configured Vitest runner first; relevant inspected examples include request.test.ts, launcher.test.ts, and node/saveScreenshot.test.ts. Broader typing, smoke, component, and e2e scripts have distinct prerequisites.

Tests and CI were inspected, not executed: carry forward the limitations that driver setup is skipped in unit tests, coverage is disabled by default, Preact/misc component commands are bypassed, and cloud CI is main-only.

Keep publication and deployment outside ordinary edits: npm publishing is manually dispatched and depends on publisher-team authorization, whereas documentation deployment is a separate manually dispatched workflow with cloud credential references.
